## Savings Account vs. Money Market vs. CD: Which Fits Your Goal?


---


### When you're saving for a big purchase, where you keep your money matters. Here's a simple guide to choosing the right account for your goals, timeline and lifestyle.


**Key takeaways:**


-


Keeping your hard-earned cash in a low-interest account means it can slowly lose its buying power over time due to inflation.


-


Savings accounts, money market accounts and CDs can help your money grow without the risks of the stock market.


-


The best option depends on when you need the cash and how easily you want to be able to pull it out.


While it’s important to keep your savings safe, being too cautious can have hidden downsides. If your money just stays in a checking or savings account with low interest, inflation can slowly erode its value.


The good news is that you don’t have to take on the risks of the stock market to put your savings to work. There are savings options that can help your money earn more without exposing it to market swings. The best choice usually comes down to when you'll need the money.


## The hidden cost of low-interest savings accounts


Putting money into a traditional checking or low-interest savings account can feel like the safest move when you’re saving for a major purchase. Your balance isn’t affected by market drops, and the money is right there when you need it. However, safety doesn’t necessarily mean your money is growing.


As of[September 2026](https://www.fdic.gov/national-rates-and-rate-caps) , the national average interest rate is 0.37% for savings accounts, and just 0.07% for interest-bearing checking accounts. If inflation is higher than the interest rate you're earning, your savings might look the same on paper, but what those dollars can actually buy goes down over time. The longer your money stays put, the wider that gap can become.


## **Where should you keep money for a big purchase?**


The best place to keep your money depends largely on your timeline. Unlike money you’re investing for retirement or long-term goals, savings for a purchase you expect to make relatively soon generally shouldn’t be exposed to significant market swings.


Instead, try to balance safety, growth and accessibility. You want your money to earn a good return, but you also need to know it will be there when it’s time to spend it.


Three common options include:


-


Savings accounts


-


Money market accounts


-


Certificates of deposit (CD)


Each offers a different balance of accessibility and earning potential. The rates, fees, balance requirements and availability of individual products can also vary, so understanding those differences can help you choose an account that fits your goal and timeline.


### **Savings account vs. money market vs. CD: What’s the difference?**


Savings accounts, money market accounts and CDs can all provide a place to earn interest on money you're setting aside for a future purchase. The main differences are how easily you can access your money, how the interest rate works and how long you’re willing to leave your savings untouched.


#### **1.** **Savings and money market accounts**


**A[savings account](https://www.northwest.bank/link/6a58c62e4035475f997e6239d759a0d5.aspx?article_source=news_insights&article_category=education&article_name=where-to-keep-money-for-a-big-purchase&article_cta=savings-account)** keeps your money separate from the cash you use for everyday expenses while still allowing you to access it when needed. You can continue contributing as you work toward your goal, making a savings account a flexible option if you’re still building your balance or don't have a firm purchase date.


Interest rates vary by account and financial institution, so it's worth comparing the annual percentage yield (APY), fees and balance requirements available to you. Some savings products may offer higher rates than others depending on the account, balance, location or other eligibility requirements.


[High-yield savings accounts](https://www.northwest.bank/link/fcf42b3a8ca242ea8b4643725a7a3d53.aspx?article_source=news_insights&article_category=education&article_name=where-to-keep-money-for-a-big-purchase&article_cta=high-yield-savings) (HYSAs), for example, are a type of savings account that generally offers a higher APY than a traditional savings account. However, product availability can vary, so a HYSA may not be an option for every saver.


#### **Best for: Short-term goals or flexible timelines**


****


A savings account can be particularly useful if you're still building toward your goal, expect to make your purchase relatively soon or aren't sure exactly when you'll need the money. Your savings can continue earning interest while remaining accessible if your plans change.


**[Money market accounts](https://www.northwest.bank/link/c1f75fc8b8934815a1a013e8e13efb37.aspx?article_source=news_insights&article_category=education&article_name=where-to-keep-money-for-a-big-purchase&article_cta=money-market-account)** offer similar benefits to savings accounts but often feature higher interest rates. Depending on the account, they may also include features like check-writing or a debit card, which can make it easier to use your savings when it's time to make your purchase.


That convenience can come with additional requirements. Some money market accounts may require a larger opening deposit or minimum balance to earn the best available rate or avoid monthly fees. Interest rates are also generally variable, meaning they can rise or fall over time.


#### **Best for: Short-to medium-term goals and customers who can meet applicable account requirements**


****


A money market account can make sense if you've already accumulated a sizable amount of money and want convenient access to your savings. It may be especially useful when features such as check-writing or debit card access would make it easier to complete your eventual purchase.


#### **2. Certificates of deposit**


A[certificate of deposit](https://www.northwest.bank/link/47ee7ea04fe0495489215a8e9a21da73.aspx?article_source=news_insights&article_category=education&article_name=where-to-keep-money-for-a-big-purchase&article_cta=certificate-of-deposit) takes a different approach. Instead of keeping your money readily accessible, you agree to leave a set amount on deposit for a specific term, which can range from a few months to several years. In return, a traditional CD typically locks in a guaranteed, fixed interest rate for the entire term.


That predictability can be useful when you know exactly when you'll need your savings. For example, if you're planning to buy a car in a year, a 12-month CD could allow you to earn a guaranteed return while you wait.


The trade-off is flexibility. Withdrawing money before the CD matures can result in an early withdrawal penalty, depending on the account.


#### **Best for: Firm timelines several months to a few years away**


****


A CD can be a strong option when you know approximately when you'll make your purchase and are confident you won't need to touch the money beforehand. Matching the CD's maturity date to your purchase timeline lets you lock in a return without tying up the money beyond when you expect to need it.


## **Find the right home for your savings**


There’s no single best place to keep money for a big purchase. The right choice depends on when you’ll need it, how easily you need access to it and the rates available to you.


Start by reviewing where your savings are today and how much interest they’re earning. Then, compare savings accounts, money market accounts and CDs based on your specific goals and timeline. Look at the minimum balance requirements, monthly fees, withdrawal restrictions and how easily you can access your money when it's time to make your purchase.


Whether you choose one account or a mix of them, moving your money to the right place can help you earn more on your savings while keeping your next big purchase within reach.
